title: Swap One Residue, Read the Result

scenes.tts: A gene is cloned; its protein is known. But which residue, tail or domain does which job? A test in a tube can miss a part whose job is to hold a partner. Before 1978 there was no widely used way to make a chosen change in a known DNA sequence. Hutchison, Smith and colleagues introduced one. Now a site can be tested: necessary, or sufficient?
scenes.visual: A cloned gene and its protein as labelled blocks with question marks on positions; a test tube reads one activity and misses a partner-holding part; a crossed-out arrow 'no general way' before 1978 becomes the 1978 method; necessary and sufficient chips.

scenes.tts: Pick the residue from a hypothesis, then choose what it becomes. Alanine cannot accept a phosphate. Aspartate has a negative charge that imitates one. A short synthetic DNA oligonucleotide, a primer, carries the change. In 1978 it was twelve bases long, matching the phi X one seven four DNA except for the change.
scenes.visual: A protein block with one marked residue; two copies with that residue swapped, one to alanine (phosphate refused) and one to aspartate (a minus sign standing in for phosphate); a twelve-letter primer under the template with one mismatched base inside the changed codon.

scenes.tts: The primer anneals to the single-stranded template. A DNA polymerase extends it around the circle, and DNA ligase seals it. Fifteen percent of progeny phage were mutants in 1978. Kunkel reached forty to sixty percent in 1985. For plasmids, the Quick Change kit copies the whole plasmid with two complementary mutant primers. D P N one then destroys the methylated parental DNA.
scenes.visual: A circle template: primer anneals, polymerase arc grows round, ligase seals; yield bars 15 percent then 40 to 60 percent; then a plasmid copied whole by two primers, and a Dpn I cut that removes the parental ring.

scenes.tts: Tyrosine to phenylalanine loses only the hydroxyl, so that tyrosine cannot be phosphorylated. A kinase-dead mutant changes the lysine that holds A T P. The receptor can still fold, pair and bind ligand, but cannot transfer phosphate. A dominant-negative receptor can lack its kinase domain. It pairs with normal partners but cannot pass the signal on. Compare the mutant with wild type under identical conditions.
scenes.visual: Three columns: Tyr to Phe, phosphate refused; kinase-dead receptor pair, ATP lysine changed, no phosphate transfer; dominant-negative receptor pairing with a normal partner and the signal stopped. Then two cells, wild-type gene and mutant gene, under the same conditions with results still unread.

Compare the mutant with wild type under identical conditions.

scenes.tts: A mutant that acts without the signal suggests sufficiency. One that blocks the normal response suggests need. In 1988 Feig and Cooper changed H-Ras serine 17 to asparagine. Its affinity for G T P fell twenty to forty fold. Cells with it formed far fewer drug-resistant colonies, so it inhibited proliferation. Activated ras reversed that. Cells with v mos or v raf resisted it, but v src cells did not. That places Ras between Src and Raf in this system.
scenes.visual: Two rows: an always-active mutant gives a response with no signal (sufficient); a blocking mutant gives no response with the signal present (needed). Then the real case: H-Ras Ser 17 to Asn, GTP affinity down, fewer colonies in schematic dishes, restored by activated ras, and v-mos, v-raf, v-src results placing Ras between Src and Raf.

Cells with v-mos or v-raf resisted it, but v-src cells did not. That places Ras between Src and Raf in this system.

scenes.tts: A mutation can damage folding or expression instead of the chosen function, so confirm expression and a retained activity. An aspartate mimic has one charge where phosphate has two, and is smaller, so add a second line of evidence, such as a kinase inhibitor. Dominant negatives work through overexpression, which can have effects beyond the intended block. Use wild-type protein at matching levels, and a rescue, which restores the blocked response.
scenes.visual: Three columns: a swapped residue that wrecks the whole protein block, control confirm expression and activity; phosphate with two charges against aspartate with one and smaller, control a kinase inhibitor; a cell flooded with mutant protein with a side effect, controls wild type at matching levels and a rescue, which restores the blocked response.

scenes.tts: In 1987 Kmiecik and Shalloway changed Src tyrosine 527 to phenylalanine. That strongly activated Src's transforming and kinase activities, and an added change at tyrosine 416 suppressed them. In 1993 Struhl, Fitzgerald and Greenwald made truncated Lin-12 and Notch with only their intracellular domains. These caused cell-fate changes associated with constitutive activity, independent of endogenous gene function.
scenes.visual: Row one: Src block, tyrosine 527 to phenylalanine turns it on, an added 416 change turns it off (Kmiecik and Shalloway 1987). Row two: a full Notch-type receptor against a truncated one that is only the intracellular part, which acts as constitutively active with no help from the endogenous gene (Struhl, Fitzgerald and Greenwald 1993).

scenes.tts: In 1994 Hemmati-Brivanlou and Melton found that a truncated activin receptor turned Xenopus explants that would become epidermal cells into neural tissue. That receptor also blocks related ligands, so it blocked more than activin. Confirm expression and activity, then add a second line of evidence.
scenes.visual: A truncated activin receptor pairs with the full one and a Xenopus explant turns from epidermis to neural (Hemmati-Brivanlou and Melton 1994), with related ligands also blocked as a caution. Then the rule in a box.
